entry:
System of legal rights giving people control over valuable things, and the things themselves. Depending on its nature, an owner may have the right to consume, alter, share, rent, sell, transfer, or destroy it, or to exclude others from doing so. Property is usually defined by the code of the local sovereignty, and the [[Judiciary|judiciary]] can adjudicate and enforce property rights. Economics and political economy distinguish four broad forms: private, public, collective, and common property. Types include real property (land and improvements to it), personal property (physical possessions), and [[Intellectual property|intellectual property]], which covers exclusive rights over artistic creations and inventions but is not always widely recognized or enforced. In sociology and anthropology, property is often defined as a relationship between individuals and an object in which at least one holds a bundle of rights over it.

Philosophers disagree about its basis: some hold that property rights arise from social convention, others find justification in morality or natural law. [[John Locke]] wrote that every man has a property in his person, and classical liberalism holds that individuals own their lives and therefore the products of them. [[Adam Smith]] tied the expectation of profit from improving one's stock of capital to private-property rights, yet also wrote that civil government, so far as it is instituted for the security of property, is in reality instituted for the defense of the rich against the poor. [[Capitalism]] assumes that property rights encourage owners to develop property, generate wealth, and allocate resources efficiently through markets. [[Conservatism]] holds that the more widespread private possession is, the more stable and productive a state becomes.

Large biomolecule consisting of one or more long chains of [[Amino acid|amino acid]] residues. Proteins catalyze metabolic reactions, replicate DNA, respond to stimuli, give structure to cells and organisms, and transport molecules. They differ mainly in their amino acid sequence, which is dictated by the nucleotide sequence of their [[Gene|genes]] and usually causes folding into a specific three-dimensional structure that determines activity. A linear chain of residues joined by peptide bonds is a polypeptide; chains shorter than 20–30 residues are rarely considered proteins and are commonly called [[Peptide|peptides]]. The genetic code specifies 20 standard amino acids, though some organisms add selenocysteine and, in certain archaea, pyrrolysine. During or shortly after synthesis, residues are often chemically modified, which alters folding, stability, activity, and function. Some proteins require a non-protein compound or ion, called a cofactor.

Synthesis, called translation, takes place on [[Ribosome|ribosomes]], where messenger RNA templates direct the assembly of amino acids. Many proteins are [[Enzyme|enzymes]] vital to metabolism. Others are structural, such as actin and myosin in [[Muscle|muscle]] and the scaffolding proteins of the cytoskeleton, or are important in cell signaling, immune responses, cell adhesion, and the cell cycle. Hemoglobin carries oxygen, and [[Insulin|insulin]] regulates metabolism. Proteins exist for minutes or years, averaging 1–2 days in mammalian cells; misfolded ones are degraded faster, often by the proteasome. Animals need dietary protein to obtain the essential amino acids they cannot make.

Proteins were first described by the Dutch chemist Gerardus Johannes Mulder and named by the Swedish chemist [[Jöns Jacob Berzelius]] in 1838, from the Greek *proteios*, "primary." Franz Hofmeister and Hermann Emil Fischer established in 1902 that proteins are chains of amino acids.

Major branch of Christianity that originated in the 16th-century [[Reformation|Protestant Reformation]]. It emphasizes justification of sinners through faith alone, salvation by unmerited divine grace, the priesthood of all believers, and the Bible as the sole infallible authority for Christian faith and practice; the five *solae* summarize mainstream Protestant belief. The Reformation began in the [[Holy Roman Empire]] in 1517, when [[Martin Luther]] published his [[Ninety-five Theses]] in reaction to abuses in the sale of indulgences by the [[Catholic Church]].

The name comes from the protest against the edict of the Diet of Speyer (1529) by six princes of the empire and the rulers of fourteen Imperial Free Cities. Lutheranism spread from Germany into Denmark–Norway, Sweden, Finland, Livonia, and Iceland. Calvinist churches, led by reformers such as [[John Calvin]], Huldrych Zwingli, and John Knox, spread in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Scotland, Switzerland, France, Poland, and Lithuania. The separation of the [[Church of England]] from Rome under Henry VIII began [[Anglicanism]].

Protestants hold to the concept of an invisible church, whereas the Catholic and Orthodox churches each regard themselves as the one true church. Major families include Anglicans/Episcopalians, Baptists, Reformed, Lutherans, Methodists, and Moravians; Adventists, Pentecostals, Quakers, and nondenominational churches may also be counted. Estimates vary with definition: Hans Hillerbrand put the Protestant population at 833,457,000 in 2004, while the World Christian Database estimated 637,856,000 Protestants and 426,370,000 Independents, most of whom do not self-identify as Protestant.

Stable subatomic particle (symbol p, H⁺) with a positive electric charge of +1 e. Its mass is slightly less than that of a [[Neutron|neutron]] and approximately 1836 times that of an electron; protons and neutrons, each about one dalton, are jointly called nucleons. One or more protons are present in the nucleus of every atom. Their number, the [[Atomic number|atomic number]] (Z), defines the element and, with the matching number of electrons, determines its chemical characteristics. The nucleus of the most common hydrogen isotope is a lone proton; deuterium and tritium contain one proton bound to one and two neutrons, respectively.

Once thought elementary, protons are composite particles in the [[Standard Model]]: spin-1/2 fermions and baryons, a kind of hadron, made of three valence [[Quark|quarks]], two up quarks of charge +2/3 e and one down quark of charge −1/3 e, held together by gluons through the [[Strong interaction|strong force]]. Quark rest masses contribute only about 1% of a proton's mass; the remainder is quantum chromodynamics binding energy.

The idea of a hydrogen-like constituent of atoms goes back to William Prout's hypothesis of 1815, and [[J. J. Thomson]] later found canal rays consistent with hydrogen ions. In 1919 [[Ernest Rutherford]] used alpha particles from radium to strike air and observed what he called artificial disintegration of nitrogen atoms; by 1920 he concluded that hydrogen nuclei were a constituent of the nitrogen nucleus, and he named the particle from the Greek for "first." Free protons are used in accelerators for proton therapy and particle physics experiments, the most powerful being the [[Large Hadron Collider]].

Scientific study of the mind and behavior. Its subject matter includes the behavior of humans and nonhumans, conscious and unconscious phenomena, and mental processes such as thoughts, feelings, and motives. It is an academic discipline of broad scope that crosses the boundaries between the natural and social sciences. A professional practitioner or researcher is called a psychologist, and some are also classed as behavioral or cognitive scientists. Biological psychologists seek to understand the emergent properties of brains, linking the field to [[Neuroscience|neuroscience]], while others, as social scientists, study the behavior of individuals and groups. Research covers perception, cognition, attention, emotion, intelligence, motivation, brain functioning, personality, interpersonal relationships, and the unconscious mind. Research psychologists use empirical methods to infer causal and correlational relationships between psychosocial variables. Psychological knowledge is applied to the assessment and treatment of mental health problems, and many psychologists practice [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]] in clinical, counseling, or school settings. Others conduct research, usually in academic settings, work in industrial and organizational settings, or study human development, aging, sports, health, forensic science, education, and the media.

The word derives from the Greek *psyche*, "spirit" or "soul," and *-logia*, "study." In its Latin form *psychiologia* it was first used by the Croatian humanist Marko Marulić between 1510 and 1520; the earliest known English use is by Steven Blankaart in 1694. In 1890 [[William James]] defined psychology as "the science of mental life, both of its phenomena and their conditions." In 1913 [[John B. Watson]] contested this, asserting a methodological [[Behaviorism|behaviorist]] view of psychology as a purely objective experimental branch of natural science whose goal is "the prediction and control of behavior."

The ancient civilizations of Egypt, Greece, China, India, and Persia all engaged in philosophical study of the mind. [[Hippocrates]] theorized that mental disorders had physical rather than supernatural causes. In Germany, Christian Wolff identified psychology as its own science, writing *Psychologia Empirica* in 1732 and *Psychologia Rationalis* in 1734, while [[Immanuel Kant]] rejected the idea of an experimental psychology. The discipline is commonly dated as an independent science from 1879, when [[Wilhelm Wundt]] established the first experimental psychology laboratory, at the University of Leipzig. Behaviorism, which prioritized observable responses over internal states, was followed in the mid-20th century by the cognitive revolution, which brought information-processing models. Cognitive-behavioral therapy is an evidence-based intervention for disorders such as depression and anxiety. Since the 2010s a replication crisis has been documented: a 2015 Open Science Collaboration project reproduced 36% of 100 studies, prompting reforms such as preregistration and open data. A 2010 analysis by Henrich, Heine, and Norenzayan noted that most research participants come from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies, raising questions about generalizing results.

Process of making information, literature, music, software, and other content available to the public, in physical or digital form, for sale or free of charge. Traditionally the term meant the creation and distribution of printed works such as books, zines, [[Comic book|comic books]], [[Newspaper|newspapers]], and [[Magazine|magazines]]. Digital systems have extended it to e-books, websites, social media, music, and [[Video game|video game]] publishing. It has evolved from a small, ancient form limited by law or religion into a large-scale modern industry. The development of movable-type printing by [[Johannes Gutenberg]] around 1440 drastically reduced costs and widened access to books.

The commercial industry ranges from multinational conglomerates such as News Corp, Pearson, Penguin Random House, and Thomson Reuters to thousands of small independent publishers. Its divisions include trade publishing of fiction and non-fiction, educational publishing, and academic and scientific publishing. "Publisher" can mean a publishing company, an organization, or an individual who leads a company, imprint, periodical, or newspaper.

Newspapers publish current reports by journalists and are usually subsidized with advertising. Academic and technical journals usually require submissions to undergo [[Peer review|peer review]]. Book publishing covers fiction and non-fiction in print, e-book, and audiobook form, and each book has a registered [[ISBN]], standardized in 1966; self-publishing is made possible by small-run digital printing and online platforms. A university press is run by a university, and Oxford University Press is the largest in the world. Print catalogs have evolved into searchable product databases known as [[E-commerce|e-commerce]]. In 2024 the U.S. industry reported $32.5 billion in aggregate revenue, and the global books market was approximately $151 billion, with print still dominating digital formats.

Founder of the Qin dynasty and first emperor of China (r. 221–210 BC). Born Ying Zheng, he became king of Qin with the help of the merchant Lü Buwei. By 221 BC he had conquered all the other [[Warring States period|warring states]] and unified China. Rather than keep the title of king, he created the title *huángdì* ("emperor"), combining the names of the mythical Three Sovereigns and legendary Five Emperors; it was used by monarchs in China and other countries for the next two millennia.

His generals added the Yue lands of Hunan and Guangdong in campaigns south of Chu and took the Ordos Plateau from the [[Xiongnu]] in Inner Asia, although the Xiongnu later rallied. With his minister [[Li Si]] he enacted economic and political reforms standardizing the diverse practices of earlier states, including weights, measures, currency, axle widths, and script, and replaced feudal lords with appointed officials. His public works included the incorporation of state walls into a single [[Great Wall of China]], a national road system, and a city-sized mausoleum guarded by the life-sized [[Terracotta Army]].

He is traditionally said to have banned and burned many books and executed scholars. He has often been portrayed as a tyrant and strict Legalist, characterizations stemming partly from the assessments of the succeeding [[Han dynasty]] and of [[Sima Qian]]. Since the mid-20th century scholars have questioned this evaluation and debated the nature of his policies. He died in 210 BC during his fifth tour of eastern China, and the [[Qin dynasty]] collapsed in 206 BC amid revolts. The sinologist Michael Loewe wrote that the achievements of his reign marked "the start of an epoch that closed in 1911."

Fundamental physical theory describing the behavior of matter and light at and below the scale of atoms. It describes systems that [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]] cannot, and classical mechanics can be derived from it as an approximation valid at ordinary scales. Bound quantum systems have energy, momentum, angular momentum, and other quantities quantized to discrete values, and measurements show characteristics of both particles and waves ([[Wave–particle duality|wave–particle duality]]). There are limits to how accurately a physical quantity can be predicted before measurement, expressed in the [[Uncertainty principle|uncertainty principle]]: no preparation allows precise prediction of both position and momentum at once.

The theory arose from observations classical physics could not explain, such as [[Max Planck]]'s 1900 solution to the black-body radiation problem and the correspondence between energy and frequency in [[Albert Einstein]]'s 1905 explanation of the photoelectric effect. The full theory developed in the mid-1920s through these men, Max Born, Paul Dirac, and others.

In one formalism, the [[Wave function|wave function]] gives probability amplitudes for the results of measurements. Under the Born rule, a probability is the square of the absolute value of a complex number, so the theory usually predicts only probabilities, not certain outcomes. Interference is illustrated by the [[Double-slit experiment|double-slit experiment]], in which light or electrons form bright and dark bands yet are absorbed at discrete points. Another non-classical effect is [[Quantum tunnelling|quantum tunnelling]], in which a particle crosses a potential barrier even if its kinetic energy is smaller than the barrier. Applications include semiconductors, lasers, and medical imaging. Interpretation, including the measurement problem, remains debated, and reconciling the theory with general relativity is an open challenge.

Central religious text of [[Islam]], believed by Muslims to be a revelation directly from God (Allāh). Its name, also romanized Qur'an or Koran, is Arabic for "the recitation." It is organized in 114 chapters (*sūrah*), made up of verses (*āyah*), and is widely regarded as the finest work in Arabic literature, having significantly influenced the Arabic language.

Muslims believe it was revealed orally by God to the final prophet, [[Muhammad]], through the angel [[Gabriel]] over some 23 years, beginning when Muhammad was 40 and concluding in 632 CE, the year of his death. They regard it as Muhammad's most important miracle and a proof of his prophethood. Many Muslim theologians have debated whether the Quran was "created or uncreated." According to tradition, companions of Muhammad served as scribes, and shortly after his death the text was compiled on the order of the first caliph, [[Abu Bakr]] (r. 632–634). Caliph [[Uthman]] (r. 644–656) established a standard version, the Uthmanic codex, generally considered the archetype of the Quran known today. Canonical variant readings (*qirāʾāt*), transmitted orally, differ in minor wording and nuance. Some scholars argue that manuscript evidence suggests a more gradual and complex process of compilation and canonization.

The Quran describes itself as a guide for humanity. It alludes to narratives found in biblical and apocryphal texts, summarizing rather than quoting them, which Islamic theorists attribute to its focus on moral lessons. The [[Hadith|hadith]], oral traditions reflecting the words and actions of Muhammad, serve for most Muslims as additional guidance, notably in establishing Islamic law. In prayers the Quran is recited only in Arabic; a person who has memorized all of it is called a *hafiz*, and some Muslims recite it entirely during the *tarawih* prayers of [[Ramadan]].

Polymeric molecule, ribonucleic acid, essential for most biological functions, either by acting itself (non-coding RNA) or by forming a template for protein production (messenger RNA). RNA and [[DNA]] are [[Nucleic acid|nucleic acids]], one of the four major macromolecule classes essential to all known life. RNA is a chain of nucleotides, each with a ribose sugar, a phosphate group, and a base: adenine, cytosine, guanine, or uracil. Adenine pairs with uracil and cytosine with guanine through hydrogen bonds. Unlike DNA, it is typically single-stranded and forms short helices packed into structures akin to those of proteins. It differs chemically from DNA by a hydroxyl group at the 2' position of the ribose, which makes the backbone prone to cleavage. Bases and sugars can be modified in numerous ways as RNAs mature.

Cellular organisms use messenger RNA (mRNA) to convey genetic information that directs synthesis of specific proteins, and many [[Virus|viruses]] have RNA genomes. In protein synthesis on [[Ribosome|ribosomes]], transfer RNA (tRNA) delivers amino acids and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) links them into coded proteins. Other RNAs catalyze reactions, control [[Gene expression|gene expression]], or sense and respond to cellular signals; the ribosome's active site is composed entirely of RNA, making it a ribozyme. Small nuclear RNAs form spliceosomes that remove introns from pre-mRNA, and microRNAs and small interfering RNAs mediate gene silencing. Dysfunctions in RNA processing are implicated in diseases such as myotonic dystrophy and certain cancers, and mRNA vaccines use RNA to encode antigens.

It is widely accepted that early in the history of life, before the evolution of DNA and possibly of protein enzymes, an "RNA world" existed in which RNA both stored genetic information and catalyzed reactions.
